criteria.descriptor: Uses the semantics of routing, quality escalation/cascade, and reliability fallback correctly and keeps them distinct; routing and confidence signals proposed are technically valid; cost accounting is sound (weighted mix, cascade double-cost, output-token/context dominance); validation methodology (offline eval set, LLM-judge/human, canary/A-B, guardrails) is correct. Deduct for errors such as treating a cascade as free, claiming public benchmark scores prove the small model is adequate, or using temperature/prompt tweaks as the routing signal.

Addresses all three asked parts — (a) how requests are routed, (b) fallback vs. escalation triggers, and (c) before-and-after validation — plus a cost/latency account and a quality guardrail/rollback. Full marks require that both reliability fallback AND quality validation are covered, not just the cost mechanism.

Justifies why each mechanism is chosen, makes the cost-vs-quality trade-off explicit, reasons about the latency/double-cost of cascades, and explains guardrails that bias uncertain or high-risk tickets toward the large model rather than asserting a design without rationale.

Clear structure that separates routing, fallback/escalation, and validation; precise use of domain vocabulary (router, cascade, failover, LLM-judge, canary/shadow); a grader can map each claim to a concrete mechanism and metric.

expected_answer_points: Distinguishes routing (upfront model choice) from reliability fallback (reactive failover on errors) from quality-based escalation/cascade (promote to the larger model when the cheap answer is weak), using the terms correctly

Specifies a cheap routing signal for difficulty — e.g. ticket category/metadata, retrieval-hit strength, query features, an embedding/small-classifier router, or a lightweight LLM router — routing easy queries to the small model and hard/high-value ones to the large model

Describes a cascade/escalation trigger based on a quality or confidence signal (judge/verifier score, self-consistency/confidence, refusal or 'unsure', or structured-output/validation failure), and notes it must be bounded
Treats reliability fallback separately: retry with exponential backoff + jitter honouring Retry-After on 429/5xx/timeout, then fail over to an alternate model/provider to preserve availability

Gives a cost/latency account: expected cost as a weighted mix of the two tiers, the extra call and latency a cascade adds on hard tickets, output-token/long-context dominance, and/or semantic caching; confirms the realised routed split against the cost target

Validates quality before rollout with a task-specific offline eval set (representative + adversarial) judged by an LLM-judge and/or humans by segment, explicitly rejecting reliance on public benchmarks alone
Validates after rollout with a canary/shadow/A-B rollout plus online quality guardrails (thumbs-down, human-escalation rate, sampled judge scores) and an automatic rollback trigger
Names the central trade-off (cost saved by down-routing vs. quality regression risk on complex tickets) and biases uncertain/high-risk cases toward the large model
common_pitfalls: Conflates reliability fallback (failover on 429/5xx/timeout) with quality-based escalation/cascade, treating them as a single mechanism
Routes or judges every request through the large model (e.g. as an LLM router or verifier on all traffic), reintroducing the cost the design was meant to remove
Assumes a cascade is free — ignores that running the small model then the large model on hard tickets costs two calls and adds latency versus going straight to the large model
Validates only cost ($/request) with no quality-regression check, or only quality with no confirmation the routed split actually hits the cost target
Relies on public leaderboards (MMLU, LMArena, etc.) to claim the small model is 'good enough' instead of a task-specific offline eval set with a judge
Picks models by parameter count or headline price alone, or tunes temperature/prompt wording as if that were the routing decision
reference_answer:
Separate three concerns that are routinely conflated.

1) Routing (proactive model choice). Classify each request's difficulty cheaply and pick a tier. Signals: ticket category/metadata, query length, whether retrieval returned strong hits, and an embedding- or small-classifier 'difficulty' score (or a lightweight LLM router). Easy/FAQ-style tickets -> small model; ambiguous, multi-step, or high-value tickets -> large model. Pin known-risky categories (billing disputes, legal) to the large model regardless.

2) Escalation/cascade (quality-based). Optionally send to the small model first and promote to the large model only when a quality signal is weak: low self-consistency/confidence, a verifier or LLM-judge score below threshold, an explicit refusal/'not sure', or a structured-output validation failure. Bound the escalation rate; a cascade costs two calls and adds latency on the hard fraction, so it only pays off if most traffic resolves at tier 1.

3) Fallback (reliability). Orthogonal to quality: on 429/5xx/timeout, retry with exponential backoff + jitter honouring Retry-After, then fail over to an alternate provider/model to preserve availability. Don't couple this to quality routing.

Cost model: expected cost ~= share_small*cost_small + share_large*cost_large (+ cascade overhead). Most spend is usually output tokens and long RAG context, so add semantic caching for repeated questions, and track the realised small/large split to confirm the ~50% target.

Validation: before rollout, build a representative + adversarial offline eval set of tickets and compare small vs large answers with a rubric-based LLM-judge plus spot human review, reporting the quality delta by segment — never rely on public leaderboards alone. Then roll out via shadow/canary or A/B with online guardrails (thumbs-down rate, human-escalation rate, sampled judge scores) and an automatic rollback if quality regresses. Bias ties toward the large model so cost savings never come at the expense of complex-ticket quality. The core trade-off is cost saved by down-routing versus quality risk on hard tickets (and the added latency/double-cost of cascades).
